title: Heaviest Window of Distinct Values
statement:
You get an array nums of positive integers. Pick one contiguous block in which no value repeats.

Return the largest possible sum of such a block.

examples.why: [2, 4, 5, 6] has no repeats and sums to 17. Adding the first 4 would repeat it.
The longest distinct block, [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], sums to only 15. The short block [5, 60] is heavier.
Every block longer than one element repeats a value.

hints: Think of a window [left, right] that never contains a repeat. When you add nums[right] and it is already inside, what must happen to left?
Move left forward, removing elements, until the old copy of nums[right] is gone. Keep a running sum of the window.
Each element enters and leaves the window at most once, so the whole scan is linear. Record the window sum after every step.

explain.intuition:
This is the classic "longest run without repeats" window, but you score a window by its sum instead of its length. All values are positive, so for a fixed right end, the window that reaches furthest left is the heaviest. That is exactly the window the sliding technique keeps.

Grow the window to the right one element at a time. If the new value is already in the window, shrink from the left, subtracting values from the running sum, until the old copy is removed. Then the window is valid again; compare its sum with the best so far.
steps: Keep a set of values in the window, a running sum, left = 0 and best = 0.
For each right: while nums[right] is in the set, remove nums[left] from the set and the sum, and move left forward.
Add nums[right] to the set and the sum.
Update best = max(best, sum). Return best at the end.
pitfalls: Returning the sum of the longest distinct block. Length and weight are different, as the second example shows.
Jumping left to just past the last copy without removing the skipped values from the set and the sum.
Relying on the window being heaviest when it is widest. That only holds because values are positive; with negatives you would need a different approach.

solutions.title: Grow from every start
solutions.idea: From each start, extend to the right until a value repeats, tracking the sum.

solutions.title: Sliding window with a set
solutions.idea: Shrink from the left until the incoming value is not inside, then add it. Track the window sum.

solutions.title: Last-seen index and prefix sums
solutions.idea: Store where each value was last seen. The left edge jumps straight past the previous copy, and a prefix sum gives the window sum in O(1).

followups: Each value may now appear at most twice in the block. What changes in the shrinking rule?
Values can be negative. Is the widest valid window still the heaviest for a fixed right end?
